4: This experiment quantified the extent to which production location, landrace and duration of post-harvest storage govern the grain quality of three traditional aromatic rices of West Bengal. The landraces examined were Gobindabhog (V1), Radhunipagal (V2) and Kalojira (V3), procured respectively from Nadia (L1), Purba Bardhaman (L2) and Birbhum/Howrah (L3). Each lot was evaluated as fresh paddy (S1) and again at 4 months (S2), 8 months (S3) and 12 months (S4) after harvest. The experiment followed a factorial randomised block design with three replications and was repeated in 2022-23 and 2023-24. Thirty-eight parameters were recorded and are presented under seven heads: physical, sensory, nutritional, anti-nutritional, colour, mineral and amino acid attributes. Data were subjected to analysis of variance appropriate to a three-factor factorial randomised block design (Das and Giri, 1986), with year incorporated as an additional factor. The year × treatment interactions proved non-significant for the majority of parameters; all means reported below are therefore pooled over the two years. SEm, CD at the 5% level and CV were computed from the pooled error mean square with 140 degrees of freedom. Means sharing a common letter do not differ significantly at the 5% level by the least significant difference test. In the tables, GB, RP and KJ denote the three landraces in the order given above. Amino acids were assayed on freshly harvested grain alone; Section 4.7 consequently reports S1 means only and records no effect of storage.
7: The main effect means for all parameters in this section are consolidated in Table 1. The individual parameters, with their interaction means, standard errors and critical differences, are presented below.

Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to -1.3% at Nadia, -1.2% at Purba Bardhaman and -1.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations changed by closely comparable margins, storage having acted upon the grain in much the same manner irrespective of where it was grown.

23: The three-factor interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 80.20% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 72.38% by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months, a spread of 7.82 percentage points. This range is appreciably wider than that generated by any single factor in isolation. Location, landrace and storage period operated jointly, and the optimum result is obtainable only by setting all three at the appropriate level.
30: Hulling is contingent upon the proportion of paddy weight represented by husk and upon the firmness with which the husk grips the kernel, both of which are determined before harvest. The proportion of husk is a varietal character, so that a landrace with a small, tightly fitting husk will invariably dehusk more readily than a bold one bearing a heavy hull; Singh et al. (2000) and Mahendra et al. (2019) recorded differences of the same order among Indian aromatic rices, and Patra et al. (2024) obtained comparable values for a West Bengal aromatic landrace. The effect of growing site is most plausibly attributable to weather during grain filling, since temperature, insolation and humidity in the weeks following flowering determine how completely the kernel fills the cavity within the husk (Li et al., 2018). Grain that fills poorly sits loosely within the hull, and a larger proportion fails to dehusk in a single pass. The change registered during storage is unlikely to represent a durable chemical alteration. Paddy exchanges moisture with the surrounding air, and a damp husk softens and grips the kernel more tightly, which is why hulling tracks the season rather than the duration of storage. Wongpornchai et al. (2004) and Zhou et al. (2002) reached the same conclusion, and Müller et al. (2022) judged the moisture balance of stored grain to be the single most decisive factor in preserving milling quality.

50: Milling recovery is determined by the resistance of the kernel to the abrasive action of the polisher. The most probable basis of the varietal differences is endosperm hardness: a bold grain with a softer endosperm fissures more readily and forfeits more material as bran and broken fragments, and Tsado et al. (2015) found cracking and breakage in milled rice to be strongly cultivar dependent. The gain observed in the early months of storage is a well documented consequence of ageing. Sulphur bridges form within the storage protein and the bond between starch and protein tightens, so that the kernel hardens and fewer grains fracture during polishing (Chrastil and Zarins, 1992; Zhou et al., 2015). This is the reason millers hold paddy for a season before polishing it. The subsequent decline most plausibly reflects moisture uptake during the humid months, which softens the grain once more, since Müller et al. (2022) concluded that both the drying history and the moisture balance of a lot govern the extent of breakage at the mill. The significance of location is likewise consistent with Li et al. (2018), who found milling outturn to respond to conditions prevailing during grain filling.

70: Head rice recovery measures the proportion of kernels surviving milling unbroken and is governed principally by kernel density and vitreousness. A small, dense, vitreous grain resists fracture, which is the most probable basis of the varietal ranking obtained here. Li et al. (2018) likewise found milling quality to be conditioned more by genotype than by growing environment, which accords with the wider spread recorded between landraces than between sites. The improvement observed during the middle period of storage is attributable to the hardening that accompanies ageing, as storage proteins polymerise and starch granules reassociate so that the kernel fractures less readily (Zhou et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2015). The subsequent forfeiture of that gain is better explained by fatigue than by chemistry: grain held through a full year absorbs and releases moisture repeatedly as the seasons turn, each cycle imposing internal stress that opens fine fissures which in time outweigh the benefit of hardening. Tsado et al. (2015) recorded the same reversal where paddy was held beyond one year in ambient storage, and Müller et al. (2022) drew the same conclusion from a broad review of post-harvest work.
